summaries.headline: Michigan House Advances Teacher Literacy Training Requirements
summaries.summary: Michigan House committee approved three bills requiring specialized literacy training for K-5 teachers and new certification candidates, responding to the state's poor reading performance where just 24% of fourth graders score proficient on national tests and only 38.9% of third graders meet state standards. The legislation would mandate teacher preparation programs include science of reading training by September 2027 and require all current elementary teachers to complete specialized literacy coursework. The bills now move to the full House as Michigan joins states nationwide overhauling how teachers learn to teach reading amid widespread student reading struggles.

summaries.headline: Half of NY Teacher Prep Programs Fail Reading Standards
summaries.summary: Half of New York's teacher preparation programs received failing grades for training educators in scientifically-based reading instruction, despite the state's push to overhaul literacy practices, according to a new National Council on Teacher Quality report. Only six of 38 evaluated programs earned A grades for teaching all five core components of reading instruction — phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension — while 19 programs failed entirely, including many in the CUNY and SUNY systems. The poor performance comes as New York's fourth-grade reading proficiency has declined sharply, with 41% of students reading at the lowest level in 2024 compared to 30% in 2013, suggesting the pipeline of new teachers may not be equipped to reverse troubling literacy trends.

summaries.headline: Teacher Prep Programs Double Science of Reading Alignment
summaries.summary: Teacher preparation programs have doubled their alignment with science of reading practices over three years, with just over half now using scientifically grounded methods to prepare new educators, according to a National Council on Teacher Quality report. The improvement from 25 percent to more than 50 percent still leaves hundreds of programs teaching outdated reading methods, with one in five earning failing grades for promoting disproven practices. The persistent gap in teacher preparation may explain why science of reading policies—now adopted in nearly every state—have yet to produce the expected gains in student reading performance.

summaries.headline: NYC Fellowship Helps Students Combat Antisemitic, Racist Thoughts
summaries.summary: A yearlong Combat Hate Fellowship in New York City pairs students from five high schools with cultural institutions and facilitated conversations to confront antisemitism, racism, and other forms of prejudice. The program, now in its second year through a partnership between the Auschwitz Jewish Center Foundation and New Visions High School District, served 27 students who later led anti-hate workshops in their own schools. The initiative addresses rising identity-based bullying, with roughly 40% of NYC middle and high school students reporting they've witnessed classmates harassed based on race, ethnicity, or religion.

summaries.headline: Colorado Districts Report Student Relief After Cellphone Bans
summaries.summary: District leaders from three Colorado school systems told the state board that cellphone bans have reduced classroom distractions, with one student telling a board member "I can breathe again" because she no longer feels compelled to check notifications constantly. The 23,000-student Colorado Springs District 11 implemented a ban in fall 2024, while Mesa County Valley School District 51 reported parents were contributing to disruptions by sending TikTok videos and coaches texting about practice during class time. The testimonies come as all 179 Colorado districts face a July 1 deadline to adopt cellphone policies, with many moving toward outright bans following Denver Public Schools' bell-to-bell prohibition approved this week.

summaries.headline: NYC Extends School Budget Protection Despite Enrollment Decline
summaries.summary: New York City schools will maintain their current funding levels for the 2026-27 school year despite projected enrollment drops, as Chancellor Kamar Samuels extends the district's "hold harmless" policy that began during the pandemic. The city has spent $1.6 billion over six years to prevent enrollment-related budget cuts while K-12 enrollment has fallen nearly 10 percent to below 800,000 students, with further declines expected. The decision delays any financial adjustment to match actual student populations, maintaining stability for principals planning staffing and programming while pushing budget realities further into the future.

summaries.headline: Michigan Cities Launch Housing, Transit Solutions for Early Childhood Educators
summaries.summary: Two Michigan cities unveiled innovative programs this week to address staffing challenges in early childhood education, with Battle Creek launching free housing for preschool educators and Grand Rapids opening a childcare center inside a transit hub. The initiatives directly target the low pay and transportation barriers that have made it difficult to recruit and retain early childhood teachers in these communities. The coordinated timing suggests districts are moving beyond traditional recruitment strategies to address the structural barriers that keep qualified educators out of the field.

summaries.headline: Denver Superintendent Marrero Seeks Miami-Dade Schools Job
summaries.summary: Denver Public Schools Superintendent Alex Marrero confirmed he is among 21 candidates for the superintendent position in Miami-Dade County Public Schools, the nation's fourth-largest district with 345,000 students. Marrero, who has led Denver's 89,000-student district since 2021 and holds a contract through 2028 with a $346,529 salary, described the application as a decision made "after thoughtful reflection on several personal and professional considerations." The move signals continued mobility among urban superintendents, with Marrero previously being considered for the Chicago Public Schools CEO role earlier this school year.

summaries.headline: Illinois Defines Play-Based Learning for Required Kindergarten
summaries.summary: Illinois lawmakers passed an official definition for play-based learning as districts prepare to implement a 2023 law requiring full-day kindergarten statewide by 2027-28. The legislation defines the practice through two types of activities: child-initiated play where students lead exploration, and teacher-guided play that connects to learning objectives — making Illinois one of the few states to formally codify such an approach. The move comes as educators nationwide push for more hands-on learning experiences amid ongoing concerns about pandemic recovery and increased screen time in classrooms.

summaries.headline: Federal Investigators Target Cherry Creek Over Race-Based Programs
summaries.summary: The Trump administration's Education Department launched a civil rights investigation into Colorado's 52,000-student Cherry Creek district, alleging the suburban Denver system uses race in student club membership, class assignments, and academic support decisions. The probe joins similar federal investigations into districts across New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago as part of a broader effort to challenge policies supporting students of color and LGBTQ students. Cherry Creek officials dispute the characterizations but say they haven't received the formal complaint, while the federal agency hasn't provided specific examples of the alleged discriminatory practices.

summaries.headline: Colorado Christian School Co-op Loses District Support
summaries.summary: Education reEnvisioned BOCES, the Colorado co-op that launched a controversial "public Christian school," lost one of its two member districts this week and may lose the second by month's end. Elizabeth School District withdrew Tuesday, and District 49 is expected to vote on exit later in June, which would leave only Pikes Peak State College as a member despite state law requiring at least one district. The membership exodus follows May legislation that sharply curtailed BOCES power to operate schools outside member districts, forcing the permanent closure of Riverstone Academy and threatening the co-op's eight remaining schools and dozens of publicly funded homeschool programs.

summaries.headline: EdTech Purchasing Sidelines Teachers Despite $30 Billion Spending
summaries.summary: American schools spent roughly $30 billion on educational technology in 2024, with projections showing that figure will nearly double by 2033, yet purchasing decisions typically originate from administrators or vendors rather than classroom teachers. School leaders routinely field constant vendor pitches and run pilots through procurement processes that feel rigorous, but these systems answer vendor-driven questions about solutions before asking teachers what problems actually need solving. Teachers closest to instruction could better identify whether classroom needs require technology platforms, schedule changes, or entirely different approaches if given authority to define the problem first rather than evaluate predetermined solutions.

summaries.headline: Rhode Island Lawmakers Create Commission to Study Funding Overhaul
summaries.summary: Rhode Island legislators advanced resolutions to establish a 15-member commission that will study recommendations from the Rhode Island Foundation's Blue Ribbon Commission, which proposed radically restructuring the state's 16-year-old school funding formula. The new commission will examine the feasibility of shifting education costs to require a much larger share of state spending, moving away from the current municipal-heavy model. Both chambers are expected to approve the measure Thursday, creating another layer of review before any actual funding changes reach districts struggling with equity gaps.

summaries.headline: Idaho Officials Launch First School Funding Formula Review Since 1990s
summaries.summary: State Superintendent Debbie Critchfield is hosting statewide listening sessions to gather input on modernizing Idaho's public school funding formula, unchanged since the 1990s. Parents and advocates highlighted an estimated $100 million special education funding gap during the first forum, while the Legislature allocated $50 million last year for private school and homeschool families instead of addressing public school needs. The feedback will inform policy legislation for the next legislative session, with officials acknowledging the current formula lacks flexibility for districts to meet local student needs.

summaries.headline: Denver Board Adopts Bell-to-Bell Cellphone Ban
summaries.summary: Denver Public Schools unanimously approved a comprehensive ban on cellphones, smartwatches, and personal devices during school hours, joining districts nationwide implementing similar restrictions to reduce classroom distractions and support student mental health. The policy requires devices to be turned off and out of sight throughout the school day, with exceptions for students needing accommodations for health, special education, or language access purposes. The move comes as Colorado districts face a July 1 deadline to establish cellphone policies under state law, though the legislation doesn't mandate outright bans.

summaries.headline: Younger Students Recover While Teens Remain Behind
summaries.summary: Nine-year-olds are performing nearly as well in reading and math as their pre-pandemic counterparts on the latest National Assessment of Educational Progress long-term trend test, but 13-year-olds who experienced elementary school disruptions continue to struggle significantly. The results, drawn from tests of over 31,000 students, show third and fourth graders rebounding while young high schoolers' reading performance matches levels from 50 years ago. The divergent outcomes suggest pandemic recovery may depend heavily on when students experienced the most severe disruptions during their academic development.

summaries.headline: Newark Gets $400K to Scale High-Impact Tutoring
summaries.summary: Newark Public Schools will receive $400,000 from New Jersey to expand high-impact tutoring — small group sessions with the same tutor three times weekly — as part of a $7.5 million statewide grant targeting districts where fewer than half of students are proficient in math and reading. The funding comes as Newark's test scores remain well below state averages, with only 34% of students passing the state English test and 21% passing math in 2025, though performance has gradually improved toward pre-pandemic levels. The investment reflects growing state recognition that intensive tutoring models show stronger research outcomes than traditional after-school programs, even as districts nationwide struggle with staffing and financing these more resource-intensive approaches.

summaries.headline: Colorado Tightens Rules for State-Funded Homeschool Programs
summaries.summary: Colorado education officials unveiled stricter regulations for state-funded homeschool enrichment programs, barring payments for private activities like ski passes, sports camps, and martial arts lessons. The new rules respond to legislative changes targeting a Monument-based co-op that authorized programs costing the state tens of millions of dollars while raising concerns about funding abuses and lack of transparency. The regulations require enrichment programs to operate under local school districts or charter schools rather than distant authorizers, ensuring offerings mirror traditional public school services.

summaries.headline: External Review Endorses District Literacy Program Despite Parent Concerns
summaries.summary: Old Saybrook Public Schools commissioned an independent review of its ARC Core Curriculum after parents questioned their children's reading progress at April board meetings. Dr. Rachael Gabriel's study, which included classroom observations, interviews, and surveys from more than 200 parents and 22 teachers, concluded the district should not abandon the program but identified areas needing adaptation and improved implementation. The timing matters since Connecticut plans to revise its approved literacy curricula list in 2027, potentially affecting ARC's status and forcing districts to navigate another transition.

summaries.headline: Berkeley Heights Board Navigates Cell Phone Rules, Privacy Concerns
summaries.summary: Berkeley Heights school board members addressed mounting parent concerns about student data privacy while preparing for state-mandated cell phone policy implementation. Parents questioned the district's use of dual monitoring systems — Securly Classroom for real-time lesson management at $8,673 annually and Gaggle for broader AI monitoring — demanding transparency about data sharing and accuracy reporting before the programs fully launch. The board's deliberations reflect the complex balance districts face between maintaining instructional focus and protecting student privacy as surveillance technology becomes standard in classrooms.

Being a teacher or an administrator has never been easy, but after the turbulence of the past two decades or so, it’s a wonder that anyone still wants to work for a public school district.

Constant uncertainty over funding, ever-changing academic requirements and social policies, and basic safety and security concerns don’t exactly create the most inviting workplaces — much less ideal learning environments for students.

As if spending your days trying to teach dozens of kids basic skills without someone putting an eye out wasn’t harrowing enough already.

For now, though, let’s set aside all the other noise and limit our focus to funding, which is by far the most pressing issue for most Yakima Valley school districts.

And it’s not just our local schools. From Sunnyside to Selah — or for that matter, from Walla Walla to Washougal — inadequate and inequitable finances are bringing many districts [to their knees](https://www.yakimaherald.com/news/local/education/state-audit-raises-concerns-with-mabton-school-districts-finances/article_721e1dda-8807-422a-8fcb-9af3b5cf292b.html).

The lion’s share of the blame for that rests with the Washington Legislature.

Earlier this year, lawmakers cut the state’s contribution to public education by $80 million during a short legislative session in Olympia. Several years before that, they mandated practices that placed even more fundamental pressure on school districts. In the 2023-25 biennium, the state allocated $30 billion for public education.

The [Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction](https://ospi.k12.wa.us/policy-funding/legislative-priorities/understanding-public-school-funding) calculates that about 78% of school districts’ funding comes from the state which, according to Washington’s constitution, is supposed to [make schools a top priority](https://leg.wa.gov/state-laws-and-rules/washington-state-constitution/?section=7ee60562-f33c-4f7c-af29-65d79a9f3892). Local taxpayers kick in about 15% of the revenues and the remaining 7% comes from the federal government.

That, however, doesn’t mean everyone gets an equal share.

The Legislature distributes funding to school districts based on a prototypical school model and the district’s enrollment numbers. The state estimates the staff, materials and resources needed to operate an average school. The state defines a school size, then calculates how many staff positions will be funded based on that size.

And while districts can ask voters to help out by floating levies to cover expenses related to student learning, the Legislature has placed tight limits on how much they can ask for.

Much of all this is an indirect result of a 2012 state Supreme Court ruling — the infamous McCleary case. The upshot of the ruling was that the state wasn’t meeting its constitutional obligation to adequately fund education.

The Legislature’s response was to draw up a new formula for school funding — one that remains largely in place now.

But it’s one that has few realistic answers for declining enrollments and sky-high costs for everything from insurance to school buses to energy costs, and it’s left local districts scratching for ways to maintain mandated functions.

At the same time, state financial help for schools continues to dwindle, despite the McCleary ruling.

Marissa Rathbone, assistant executive director of government relations for the Washington Association of School Administrators, summed it up [this way](https://www.yakimaherald.com/news/local/education/yakima-superintendents-say-changes-during-the-legislative-session-will-hurt-school-districts/article_8389434e-bae7-43fb-87f5-266b98ef9a86.html) in a recent email with the YH-R’s Alexander Banks:

“The concern is not simply how much money is in the system overall, but whether the state is meeting its obligation to support schools.”

What would help?

Modifying statewide strategies to guarantee secure and equitable funding that would stop short-shrifting rural districts.

Yes, it’s admirable that local voters have been as supportive as they have about [school bonds](https://www.yakimaherald.com/news/local/education/yakima-school-bond-officially-approved-with-officials-discussing-next-steps/article_54602590-30fb-4f4e-b2ff-9123135463a3.html) and [levies](https://www.yakimaherald.com/news/local/education/toppenish-school-levy-passing-with-66-support/article_23cd535e-e969-11ef-ba36-3b7787e26104.html). But placing heavier burdens on local taxpayers won’t dig us out of this.

Placing unfair blame on local school boards or administrators won’t either.

This one’s up to state leaders to fix, and it can’t wait. Next session, lawmakers must develop a bipartisan strategy to meet their legal responsibility to the constitution — as well as their moral obligation to Washington’s children.

They have to get it right this time.

Over £70 million of school funding is being lost annually across Westmorland and Furness Council due to undersubscription.

The [deficit](https://www.nwemail.co.uk/news/26170400.council-danger-section-114-notice-officers-warn/?ref=ed_direct) comes against a background of declining pupil numbers in schools across the area.

A report prepared for the council’s audit committee on Friday, June 12, reads that, in the 2025/26 school year, 4,173 of 18,279 primary school places were empty – over a fifth of places, 22.8 per cent of them.

But director of children’s services, [Milorad Vasic](https://www.nwemail.co.uk/news/26027091.96-per-cent-westmorland-furness-get-top-choice-school/?ref=ed_direct) , who authored the report, says the empty places are forecast to increase to 5,596 by 2029/30 – almost a third of places, at 30.6 per cent.

The council says this equates to a loss of funding of £33.5 million to primary schools each year, with each primary school place given around £6,000 in funding.

In secondary schools, of 17,286 available places, 5,182 were empty in 2025/26, with the surplus capacity predicted to rise to 5,252 – just over 30 per cent of places.

Each secondary school place gets around £7,000 in funding, equating to a loss of £36.7 million of funding yearly.

This comes as school balances are in deficit across Westmorland and Furness, with the council saying there is an overall deficit of £9.16m.

The report reads that only five local authorities in the country have overall deficits on their school balances, and that deficits ‘must be recovered within three years’.

Schools cite challenges in their budgets including falling pupil numbers and a ‘high proportion’ of SEN pupils.

School students _(Image: PA)_

### Other factors in deficit

But the author said that, while the fall in pupil numbers is a ‘key factor’ in the deficit, that there are other factors too.

The council also said in the report that it acknowledged there is ‘high anxiety’ amongst headteachers regarding school finances and deficits.

Another issue reads: “Prior to local government restructure there was a culture that when schools went into deficit, no action was taken and the school deficit balance policy was not fully adhered to.

“This meant that the school system was aware of large deficit balances against two schools which have been there for years with no action. This is highly unusual.”

But the author said that since restructure, the council has changed the relationship between it and schools, including improving communication systems and the ‘effectiveness’ of its statutory duties.

It added that a school deficit policy was implemented for the first time in 2024, having since been ‘reviewed and strengthened’.

The two schools with ‘exceptionally high deficits’ mentioned are said to have had them for a ‘number of years’.

The report reads: “One of these schools has a small sixth form and challenges with their building, the other has an exceptionally large sixth form but again challenges with their building.”

The author added that the size of schools contributes, with many being of a small capacity due to their rural location, resulting in reduced economies of scale – meaning it is harder to increase funding by increasing size.

Other issues considered included the fact that if a school which is in deficit is closed and children moved to other schools, though it will increase funding at those schools, the deficit would be transferred to the council.

Despite County Executive Steuart Pittman’s best efforts to fund the Board of Education’s budget request this year, the proposed FY27 county budget falls short of what our students deserve. Students are coming to school needing more social-emotional support and requiring more special education services, especially for autism and speech impairment. Early elementary students’ emotional dysregulation is causing sharply increased challenging behaviors — and with them, classroom disruptions and, at times, injuries to educators.

This is why the Teachers Association of Anne Arundel County urges the County Council to fully fund all of the 82.2 requested special education positions, which include classroom teachers, specialists, technicians, teaching assistants, occupational and physical therapists and speech language pathologists. Fortunately, after hearing directly from our elementary educators, Pittman made sure to include 26 of these positions in his proposed budget. However, more than half of the remaining unfunded positions have been previously paid for through Medicaid, and the school system is anticipating Medicaid cuts later this year due to the president’s so-called “Big Beautiful Bill.” This is why permanent funding must be found to maintain these positions moving forward. Unfortunately, the county executive’s budget proposal does not do this. As a result, AACPS’s contingency plan is to fill in the gap by reallocating positions that could have been used as general education classroom teachers for the next school year, which will lead to further increased class sizes. Additionally, this budget does not include other requested positions that often support our most vulnerable students: one social worker, school psychologist, pupil personnel worker, school counselor and 10 English language development teachers.

Even with significant increases, this education budget essentially maintains the status quo. Educators are glad that we are not facing staffing cuts as in neighboring counties, but this year’s funding does not move our school system “from good to great” as Superintendent Mark Bedell aims to do. Unfortunately, this budget not only must account for diminishing Medicaid funds but also a loss of $25 million in state funding. Meanwhile, the costs of running the school system — including electricity and gasoline as well as employee healthcare — are rising.

Just like the district, educators are struggling with the current affordability crisis. We appreciate that Pittman made a commitment over his two terms to increase educator pay, which has allowed AACPS to successfully recruit and retain educators; however, this year’s proposed 2.25% COLA is less than the 3% requested by the Board of Education and also falls below the rate of inflation.

It is not too late to act. If our councilmembers are willing to collaborate with the county executive, there are ways they can raise the revenue needed for our schools. There are a variety of options to consider. Those doing the best in this economy — individuals making $400,000 or more — can pay their fair share by having their income tax hit the cap of 3.3% (an increase of just 0.1%). They can explore adjustments to the progressive income tax brackets, so others doing well in this economy also pay their fair share. They could also reconsider the proposed property tax decrease, which is forced by the revenue cap, since there is an exemption if the money goes towards funding schools. Right now, the proposed tax decrease is 0.9%. Even reducing this decrease by a few tenths of a percent would generate millions of dollars for our schools.

There are creative solutions to be found if our county leaders have the political courage to do so. We urge them to meet the moment in order to generate the school funding that our students and educators deserve.

_Kristina Korona is president of the Teachers Association of Anne Arundel County._
